entries.00c412fde7b7aa677bdf1d0598f27462aca60ddd: <div sID="gen6716" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="1Kgs.10" sID="1Kgs.10"/> <div eID="gen6716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6717" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6718" type="x-p"/> Still Solomon looks great, and every thing in this chapter adds to his magnificence. We read nothing indeed of his charity, of no hospitals he built, or alms-houses; he made his kingdom so rich that it did not need them; yet, no question, many poor were relieved from the abundance of his table. A church he had built, never to be equalled; schools or colleges he need not build any, his own palace is an academy, and his court a rendezvous of wise and learned men, as well as the centre of all the circulating riches of that part of the world. I. What abundance of wisdom there was there appears from the application the queen of Sheba made to him, and the great satisfaction she had in her entertainment there (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.1-1Kgs.10.13">ver. 1-13</reference>), and others likewise, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.24">ver. 24</reference>. II. What abundance of wealth there was there appears here by the gold imported, with other things, yearly (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.14-1Kgs.10.15">ver. 14, 15</reference>), and in a triennial return, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.22">ver. 22</reference>. Gold presented (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.25">ver. 25</reference>), and gold used in targets and shields (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.16-1Kgs.10.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>), and vessels, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.21">ver. 21</reference>. A stately throne made, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.18-1Kgs.10.20">ver. 18-20</reference>. His chariots and horsemen, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.26">ver. 26</reference>. His trade with Egypt, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.28-1Kgs.10.29">ver. 28, 29</reference>. And the great plenty of silver and cedars among his people, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.27">ver. 27</reference>. So that, putting all together, it must be owned, as it is here said (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.23">ver. 23</reference>), that "king Solomon exceeded all the kings of the earth for riches, and for wisdom." Yet what was he to the King of kings? Where Christ is, by his word and Spirit, "Behold, a greater than Solomon is there."
entries.c771916a4195e8b34aaffe36013e895e0d3913ea: <div eID="gen6718" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6717" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Visit of the Queen of Sheba. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 990.)</title> <div sID="gen6719" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , she came to prove him with hard questions. <hi type="super">2</hi> And she came to Jerusalem with a very great train, with camels that bare spices, and very much gold, and precious stones: and when she was come to Solomon, she communed with him of all that was in her heart. <hi type="super">3</hi> And Solomon told her all her questions: there was not <hi type="italic">any</hi> thing hid from the king, which he told her not. <hi type="super">4</hi> And when the queen of Sheba had seen all Solomon's wisdom, and the house that he had built, <hi type="super">5</hi> And the meat of his table, and the sitting of his servants, and the attendance of his ministers, and their apparel, and his cupbearers, and his ascent by which he went up unto the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; there was no more spirit in her. <hi type="super">6</hi> And she said to the king, It was a true report that I heard in mine own land of thy acts and of thy wisdom. <hi type="super">7</hi> Howbeit I believed not the words, until I came, and mine eyes had seen <hi type="italic">it:</hi> and, behold, the half was not told me: thy wisdom and prosperity exceedeth the fame which I heard. <hi type="super">8</hi> Happy <hi type="italic">are</hi> thy men, happy <hi type="italic">are</hi> these thy servants, which stand continually before thee, <hi type="italic">and</hi> that hear thy wisdom. <hi type="super">9</hi> Blessed be the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, which delighted in thee, to set thee on the throne of Israel: because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> loved Israel for ever, therefore made he thee king, to do judgment and justice. <hi type="super">10</hi> And she gave the king a hundred and twenty talents of gold, and of spices very great store, and precious stones: there came no more such abundance of spices as these which the queen of Sheba gave to king Solomon. <hi type="super">11</hi> And the navy also of Hiram, that brought gold from Ophir, brought in from Ophir great plenty of almug trees, and precious stones. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the king made of the almug trees pillars for the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and for the king's house, harps also and psalteries for singers: there came no such almug trees, nor were seen unto this day. <hi type="super">13</hi> And king Solomon gave unto the queen of Sheba all her desire, whatsoever she asked, beside <hi type="italic">that</hi> which Solomon gave her of his royal bounty. So she turned and went to her own country, she and her servants. <div eID="gen6719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6720" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the visit which the queen of Sheba made to Solomon, no doubt when he was in the height of his piety and prosperity. Our Saviour calls her <hi type="italic">the queen of the south,</hi> for Sheba lay south of Canaan. The common opinion is that it was in Africa; and the Christians in Ethiopia, to this day, are confident that she came from their country, and that Candace was her successor, who is mentioned <reference osisRef="Acts.8.27">Acts viii. 27</reference>. But it is more probable that she came from the south part of Arabia the happy. It should seem she was a queen regent, sovereign of her country. Many a kingdom would have been deprived of its greatest blessings if a Salique law had been admitted into its constitution. Observe, <div eID="gen6720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6721" type="x-p"/> I. On what errand the queen of Sheba came—not to treat of trade or commerce, to adjust the limits of their dominions, to court his alliance for their mutual strength or his assistance against some common enemy, which are the common occasions of the congress of crowned heads and their interviews, but she came, 1. To satisfy her curiosity; for she had heard of his fame, especially for wisdom, and she came to prove him, whether he was so great a man as he was reported to be, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.1">v. 1</reference>. Solomon's fleet sailed near the coast of her country, and probably might put in there for fresh water; perhaps it was thus that <hi type="italic">she heard of the fame of Solomon,</hi> that he excelled in wisdom all the children of the east, and nothing would serve her but she would go herself and know the truth of the report. 2. To receive instruction from him. She came to <hi type="italic">hear his wisdom,</hi> and thereby to improve her own (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.42">Matt. xii. 42</reference>), that she might be the better able to govern her own kingdom by his maxims of policy. Those whom God has called to any public employment, particularly in the magistracy and ministry, should, by all means possible, be still improving themselves in that knowledge which will more and more qualify them for it, and enable them to discharge their trust well. But, it should seem, that which she chiefly aimed at was to be instructed in the things of God. She was religiously inclined, and had heard not only of the fame of Solomon, but <hi type="italic">concerning the name of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.1">v. 1</reference>), the great name of that God whom Solomon worshipped and from whom he received his wisdom, and with this God she desired to be better acquainted. Therefore does our Saviour mention her enquiries after God, by Solomon, as an aggravation of the stupidity of those who enquire not after God by our Lord Jesus Christ, though he, having lain in his bosom, was much better able to instruct them. <div eID="gen6721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6722" type="x-p"/> II. With what equipage she came, with a very great retinue, agreeable to her rank, intending to try Solomon's wealth and generosity, as well as his wisdom, what entertainment he could and would give to a royal visitant, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.2">v. 2</reference>. Yet she came not as one begging, but brought enough to bear her charges, and abundantly to recompense Solomon for his attention to her, nothing mean or common, but gold, and precious stones, and spices, because she came to trade for wisdom, which she would purchase at any rate. <div eID="gen6722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6723" type="x-p"/> III. What entertainment Solomon gave her. He despised not the weakness of her sex, blamed her not for leaving her own business at home to come so long a journey, and put herself and him to so much trouble and expense merely to satisfy her curiosity; but he made her welcome and all her train, gave her liberty to put all her questions, though some perhaps were frivolous, some captious, and some over-curious; he allowed her to <hi type="italic">commune with him of all that was in her heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.2">v. 2</reference>) and gave her a satisfactory answer to <hi type="italic">all her questions</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.3">v. 3</reference>), whether natural, moral, political, or divine. Were they designed to try him? he gave them such turns as abundantly satisfied her of his uncommon knowledge. Were they designed for her own instruction? (as we suppose most of them were), she received abundant instruction from him, and he made things surprisingly easy which she apprehended insuperably difficult, and satisfied her that there was <hi type="italic">a divine sentence in the lips of</hi> this <hi type="italic">king.</hi> But he informed her no doubt, with particular care, concerning God, and his law and instituted worship. He had taken it for granted (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.42">ch. viii. 42</reference>) that <hi type="italic">strangers would hear of his great name,</hi> and would come thither to enquire after him; and now that so great a stranger came we may be sure he was not wanting to assist and encourage her enquiries, and give her a description of the temple, and the officers and services of it, that she might be persuaded to serve the Lord whom she now sought. <div eID="gen6723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6724" type="x-p"/> IV. How she was affected with what she saw and heard in Solomon's court. Divers things are here mentioned which she admired, the buildings and furniture of his palace, the provision that was made very day for his table (when she saw that perhaps she wondered where there were mouths for all that meat, but when she saw the multitude of his attendants and guests she was as ready to wonder where was the meat for all those mouths), the orderly sitting of his servants, every one in his place, and the ready attendance of his ministers, without any confusion, their rich liveries, and the propriety with which his cup-bearers waited at his table. These things she admired, as adding much to his magnificence. But, above all these, the first thing mentioned (which contained all) is his wisdom (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.4">v. 4</reference>), of the transcendency of which she now had incontestable proofs: and the last thing mentioned, which crowned all, is his piety, the <hi type="italic">ascent by which he went up to the house of the Lord,</hi> with what gravity and seriousness, and an air of devotion in his countenance, he appeared, when he went to the temple to worship God, with as much humility then as majesty at other times. Many of the ancient versions read it, The <hi type="italic">burnt-offerings which he offered in the house of the Lord;</hi> she observed with what a generous bounty he brought his sacrifices, and with what a pious fervour he attended the offering of them; never did she see so much goodness with so much greatness. Every thing was so surprising that there was no more spirit in her, but she stood amazed; she had never seen the like. <div eID="gen6724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6725" type="x-p"/> V. How she expressed herself upon this occasion. 1. She owned her expectation far out-done, though it was highly raised by the report she heard, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.6-1Kgs.10.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. She is far from repenting her journey or calling herself a <hi type="italic">fool</hi> for undertaking it, but acknowledges it was well worth her while to come so far for the sight of that which she could not believe the report of. Usually things are represented to us, both by common fame and by our own imagination, much greater than we find them when we come to examine them; but here the truth exceeded both fame and fancy. Those who, through grace, are brought to experience the delights of communion with God will say that the one-half was not told them of the pleasures of Wisdom's ways and the advantages of her gates. Glorified saints, much more, will say that it was a true report which they heard of the happiness of heaven, but that the thousandth part was not told them, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.9">1 Cor. ii. 9</reference>. 2. She pronounced those happy that constantly attended him, and waited on him at table: "<hi type="italic">Happy are thy men, happy are these thy servants</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.8">v. 8</reference>); they may improve their own wisdom by hearing thine." She was tempted to envy them and to which herself one of them. Note, It is a great advantage to be in good families, and to have opportunity of frequent converse with those that are wise, and good, and communicative. Many have this happiness who know not how to value it. With much more reason may we say this of Christ's servants, <hi type="italic">Blessed are those that dwell in his house, they will be still praising him.</hi> 3. She blessed God, the giver of Solomon's wisdom and wealth, and the author of his advancement, who had made him king, (1.) In kindness to him, that he might have the larger opportunity of doing good with his wisdom: He <hi type="italic">delighted in thee, to set thee on the throne of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.9">v. 9</reference>. Solomon's preferment began in the prophet's calling him <hi type="italic">Jedidiah, because the Lord loved him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.25">2 Sam. xii. 25</reference>. It more than doubles our comforts if we have reason to hope they come from God's delight in us. <hi type="italic">It was his pleasure concerning thee</hi> (so it may be read) to <hi type="italic">set thee on the throne,</hi> not for thy merit's sake, but because it so seemed good unto him. (2.) In kindness to the people, <hi type="italic">because the Lord loved Israel for ever,</hi> designed them a lasting bliss, long to survive him that laid the foundations of it. "He has made thee king, not that thou mayest live in pomp and pleasure, and do what thou wilt, but <hi type="italic">to do judgment and justice.</hi>" This she kindly reminded Solomon of, and no doubt he took it kindly. Both magistrates and ministers must be more solicitous to do the duty of their places than to secure the honours and profits of them. To this she attributes his prosperity, not to his wisdom, for bread is not always <hi type="italic">to the wise</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.11">Eccl. ix. 11</reference>), but whoso <hi type="italic">doeth judgment and justice,</hi> it shall be <hi type="italic">well with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.22.15">Jer. xxii. 15</reference>. Thus <hi type="italic">giving of thanks</hi> must be <hi type="italic">made for kings,</hi> for good kings, for such kings; they are what God makes them to be. <div eID="gen6725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6726" type="x-p"/> VI. How they parted. 1. She made a noble present to Solomon of <hi type="italic">gold and spices,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.10">v. 10</reference>. David had foretold concerning Solomon that <hi type="italic">to him should be given of the gold of Sheba,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.72.15">Ps. lxxii. 15</reference>. The present of gold and spices which the wise men of the east brought to Christ was signified by this, <reference osisRef="Matt.2.11">Matt. ii. 11</reference>. Thus she paid for the wisdom she had learned and did not think she bought it dearly. Let those that are taught of God give him their hearts, and the present will be more acceptable than this of gold and spices. Mention is made of the great abundance Solomon had of his own, notwithstanding she presented and he accepted this gold. What we present to Christ he needs not, but will have us so to express our gratitude. The almug-trees are here spoken of (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.11-1Kgs.10.12">v. 11, 12</reference>) as extraordinary, because perhaps much admired by the queen of Sheba. 2. Solomon was not behind-hand with her: <hi type="italic">He gave her whatsoever, she asked,</hi> patterns, we may suppose, of those things that were curious, by which she might make the like; or perhaps he gave her his precepts of wisdom and piety in writing, <hi type="italic">besides that which he gave her of his royal bounty,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.13">v. 13</reference>. Thus those who apply to our Lord Jesus will find him not only greater than Solomon, and wiser, but more kind; whatsoever we ask, it shall be done for us; nay, he will, out of his divine bounty, which infinitely exceeds royal bounty, even Solomon's, do for us <hi type="italic">more than we are able to ask or think.</hi>
entries.9a61e42ba7b8c93a6c2ba86b0f4fe537fa31c983: <div eID="gen6726" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Solomon's Wealth. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 990.)</title> <div sID="gen6727" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was six hundred threescore and six talents of gold, <hi type="super">15</hi> Beside <hi type="italic">that he had</hi> of the merchantmen, and of the traffick of the spice merchants, and of all the kings of Arabia, and of the governors of the country. <hi type="super">16</hi> And king Solomon made two hundred targets <hi type="italic">of</hi> beaten gold: six hundred <hi type="italic">shekels</hi> of gold went to one target. <hi type="super">17</hi> And <hi type="italic">he made</hi> three hundred shields <hi type="italic">of</hi> beaten gold; three pound of gold went to one shield: and the king put them in the house of the forest of Lebanon. <hi type="super">18</hi> Moreover the king made a great throne of ivory, and overlaid it with the best gold. <hi type="super">19</hi> The throne had six steps, and the top of the throne <hi type="italic">was</hi> round behind: and <hi type="italic">there were</hi> stays on either side on the place of the seat, and two lions stood beside the stays. <hi type="super">20</hi> And twelve lions stood there on the one side and on the other upon the six steps: there was not the like made in any kingdom. <hi type="super">21</hi> And all king Solomon's drinking vessels <hi type="italic">were of</hi> gold, and all the vessels of the house of the forest of Lebanon <hi type="italic">were of</hi> pure gold; none <hi type="italic">were of</hi> silver: it was nothing accounted of in the days of Solomon. <hi type="super">22</hi> For the king had at sea a navy of Tharshish with the navy of Hiram: once in three years came the navy of Tharshish, bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks. <hi type="super">23</hi> So king Solomon exceeded all the kings of the earth for riches and for wisdom. <hi type="super">24</hi> And all the earth sought to Solomon, to hear his wisdom, which God had put in his heart. <hi type="super">25</hi> And they brought every man his present, vessels of silver, and vessels of gold, and garments, and armour, and spices, horses, and mules, a rate year by year. <hi type="super">26</hi> And Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen: and he had a thousand and four hundred chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen, whom he bestowed in the cities for chariots, and with the king at Jerusalem. <hi type="super">27</hi> And the king made silver <hi type="italic">to be</hi> in Jerusalem as stones, and cedars made he <hi type="italic">to be</hi> as the sycamore trees that <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the vale, for abundance. <hi type="super">28</hi> And Solomon had horses brought out of Egypt, and linen yarn: the king's merchants received the linen yarn at a price. <hi type="super">29</hi> And a chariot came up and went out of Egypt for six hundred <hi type="italic">shekels</hi> of silver, and a horse for a hundred and fifty: and so for all the kings of the Hittites, and for the kings of Syria, did they bring <hi type="italic">them</hi> out by their means. <div eID="gen6727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6728" type="x-p"/> We have here a further account of Solomon's prosperity. <div eID="gen6728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6729" type="x-p"/> I. How he increased his wealth. Though he had much, he still coveted to have more, being willing to try the utmost the things of this world could do to make men happy. 1. Besides the gold that came from Ophir (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.28">ch. ix. 28</reference>), he brought so much into his country from other places that the whole amounted, every year, to 666 <hi type="italic">talents</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.14">v. 14</reference>), an ominous number, compare <reference osisRef="Rev.13.18">Rev. xiii. 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.13">and Ezra ii. 13</reference>. 2. He received a great deal in customs from the merchants, and in land-taxes from the countries his father had conquered and made tributaries to Israel, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.15">v. 15</reference>. 3. He was Hiram's partner in a Tharshish fleet, of and for Tyre, which imported once in three years, not only gold, and silver, and ivory, substantial goods and serviceable, but apes to play with and peacocks to please the eye with their feathers, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.22">v. 22</reference>. I wish this may not be an evidence that Solomon and his people, being overcharged with prosperity, by this time grew childish and wanton. 4. He had presents made him, every year, from the neighbouring princes and great men, to engage the continuance of his friendship, not so much because they feared him or were jealous of him as because they loved him and admired his wisdom, had often occasion to consult him as an oracle, and sent him these presents by way of recompence for his advice in politics, and (whether it became his grandeur and generosity or no we will not enquire) he took all that came, even garments and spices, horses and mules, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.24-1Kgs.10.25">v. 24, 25</reference>. 5. He traded to Egypt for horses and linen-yarn (or, as some read it, <hi type="italic">linen-cloth</hi>), the staple commodities of that country, and had his own merchants or factors whom he employed in this traffic and who were accountable to him, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.28-1Kgs.10.29">v. 28, 29</reference>. The custom to be paid to the king of Egypt for exported chariots and horses out of Egypt was very high, but (as bishop Patrick understands it) Solomon, having married his daughter, got him to compound for the customs, so that he could bring them up cheaper than his neighbours, which obliged them to buy them of him, which he was wise enough no doubt to make his advantage of. This puts an honour upon the trading part of a nation, and sets a tradesman not so much below a gentleman as some place him, that Solomon, one of the greatest men that ever was, thought it no disparagement to him to deal in trade. In all labour there is profit. <div eID="gen6729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6730" type="x-p"/> II. What use he made of his wealth. He did not hoard it up in his coffers, that he might have it to look upon and leave behind him. He has, in his Ecclesiastes, so much exposed the folly of hoarding that we cannot suppose he would himself be guilty of it. No, God that had given him riches, and wealth, and honour, gave him also power to eat thereof, and to take his portion, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.19">Eccles. v. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen6730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6731" type="x-p"/> 1. He laid out his gold in fine things for himself, which he might the better be allowed to do when he had before laid out so much in fine things for the house of God. (1.) He made 200 targets, and 300 shields, of beaten gold (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.16-1Kgs.10.17">v. 16, 17</reference>), not for service, but for state, to be carried before him when he appeared in pomp. With us, magistrates have <hi type="italic">swords</hi> and <hi type="italic">maces</hi> carried before them, as the Romans had their <hi type="italic">rods</hi> and <hi type="italic">axes,</hi> in token of their power to correct and punish the bad, to whom they are to be a terror. But Solomon had <hi type="italic">shields</hi> and <hi type="italic">targets</hi> carried before him, to signify that he took more pleasure in using his power for the defence and protection of the good, to whom he would be a praise. Magistrates are <hi type="italic">shields of the earth.</hi> (2.) He made a stately throne, on which he sat, to give laws to his subjects, audience to ambassadors, and judgment upon appeals, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.18-1Kgs.10.20">v. 18-20</reference>. It was made of ivory, or elephants' teeth, which was very rich; and yet, as if he had so much gold that he knew not what to do with it, he <hi type="italic">overlaid that with gold,</hi> the best gold. Yet some think he did not cover the ivory all over, but here and there. He rolled it, flowered it, or inlaid it, with gold. The stays or arms of this stately chair were supported by the images of lions in gold; so were the steps and paces by which he went up to it, to be a memorandum to him of that courage and resolution wherewith he ought to execute judgment, not fearing the face of man. <hi type="italic">The righteous,</hi> in that post, <hi type="italic">is bold as a lion.</hi> (3.) He made all his drinking vessels, and all the furniture of his table, even at his country seat, of pure gold, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.21">v. 21</reference>. He did not grudge himself what he had, but took the credit and comfort of it, such as it was. That is good that does us good. <div eID="gen6731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6732" type="x-p"/> 2. He made it circulate among his subjects, so that the kingdom was as rich as the king; for he had no separate interests of his own to consult, but sought the welfare of his people. Those princes are not governed by Solomon's maxims who think it policy to keep their subjects poor. Solomon was herein a type of Christ, who is not only rich himself, but enriches all that are his. Solomon was instrumental to bring so much gold into the country, and disperse it, that <hi type="italic">silver was nothing accounted of,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.21">v. 21</reference>. There was such plenty of it in Jerusalem that it was as the stones; and cedars, that used to be great rarities, were as common <hi type="italic">as sycamore trees,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.27">v. 27</reference>. Such is the nature of worldly wealth, plenty of it makes it the less valuable; much more should the enjoyment of spiritual riches lessen our esteem of all earthly possessions. If <hi type="italic">gold in abundance</hi> would make silver to seem so despicable, shall not wisdom, and grace, and the foretastes of heaven, which are far better than gold, make earthly wealth seem much more despicable? <div eID="gen6732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6733" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Well, thus rich, thus great, was Solomon, and thus did he <hi type="italic">exceed all the kings of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.23">v. 23</reference>. Now let us remember, 1. That this was he who, when he was <hi type="italic">setting out in the world,</hi> did not ask for the wealth and honour of it, but asked for <hi type="italic">a wise and understanding heart.</hi> The more moderate our desires are towards earthly things the better qualified we are for the enjoyment of them and the more likely to have them. See, in Solomon's greatness, the performance of God's promise (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.3.13">ch. iii. 13</reference>), and let it encourage us to <hi type="italic">seek first the righteousness of God's kingdom.</hi> 2. That this was he who, having tasted all these enjoyments, wrote a whole book to show the vanity of all worldly things and the vexation of spirit that attends them, their insufficiency to make us happy and the folly of setting our hearts upon them, and to recommend to us the practice of serious godliness, as that which is the whole of man, and will do infinitely more towards the making of us easy and happy than all the wealth and power that he was master of, and which, through the grace of God, is within our reach, when the thousandth part of Solomon's greatness is a thousand times more than we can ever be so vain as to promise ourselves in this world.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.10"/> <div eID="gen6733" type="x-p"/>

entries.0fbe30cb2887a3113e328570b2a1649f062442a5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3192"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <div sID="gen4459" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.1-1Kgs.10.13">1Ki 10:1-13</reference>. The Queen of Sheba Admires the Wisdom of Solomon.<div eID="gen4459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4460" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3192"/><hi type="bold">1. the queen of Sheba--</hi>Some think her country was the Sabean kingdom of Yemen, of which the capital was Saba, in Arabia-Felix; others, that it was in African Ethiopia, that is, Abyssinia, towards the south of the Red Sea. The opinions preponderate in favor of the former. This view harmonizes with the language of our Lord, as Yemen means "South"; and this country, extending to the shores of the Indian ocean, might in ancient times be considered "the uttermost parts of the earth."<div eID="gen4460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4461" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heard of the fame of Solomon--</hi>doubtless by the Ophir fleet.<div eID="gen4461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4462" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">concerning the name of the Lord--</hi>meaning either his great knowledge of God, or the extraordinary things which God had done for him.<div eID="gen4462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4463" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hard questions--</hi>enigmas or riddles. The Orientals delight in this species of intellectual exercise and test wisdom by the power and readiness to solve them. <div eID="gen4463" type="x-p"/>
entries.8cf27095f3cd58a20b78fd181612507c7a82b7aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3193"/><div sID="gen4464" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3193"/><hi type="bold">2. she came to Jerusalem with a very great train, with camels--</hi>A long train of those beasts of burden forms the common way of travelling in Arabia; and the presents specified consist of the native produce of that country. Of course, a royal equipage would be larger and more imposing than an ordinary caravan. <div eID="gen4464" type="x-p"/>
entries.585be000edc24a58379fb955f8bd189d10a99ab1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3194"/><div sID="gen4465" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3194"/><hi type="bold">6. It was a true report that I heard in mine own land of thy acts and of thy wisdom--</hi>The proofs she obtained of Solomon's wisdom--not from his conversation only, but also from his works; the splendor of his palace; the economy of his kitchen and table; the order of his court; the gradations and gorgeous costume of his servants; above all, the arched viaduct that led from his palace to the temple (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.18">2Ki 16:18</reference>), and the remains of which have been recently discovered [Robinson]--overwhelmed her with astonishment. [See on <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.4">2Ch 9:4</reference>.] <div eID="gen4465" type="x-p"/>
entries.479b750585dd947906dd0f11c6beb5372ad1c225: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3195"/><div sID="gen4466" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3195"/><hi type="bold">9. Blessed be the Lord thy God--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.7">1Ki 5:7</reference>). It is quite possible, as Jewish writers say, that this queen was converted, through Solomon's influence, to the worship of the true God. But there is no record of her making any gift or offering in the temple. <div eID="gen4466" type="x-p"/>
entries.8839b7026d69e6a8d02f22fd9937f47c1e2f0b79: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3196"/><div sID="gen4467" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3196"/><hi type="bold">10. she gave the king an hundred and twenty talents of gold--</hi>£720,00. <div eID="gen4467" type="x-p"/>
entries.84181cc7023d15c296f4d61aa5ffe099ec8d3f0f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3197"/><div sID="gen4468" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3197"/><hi type="bold">11. almug trees--</hi>Parenthetically, along with the valuable presents of the queen of Sheba, is mentioned a foreign wood, which was brought in the Ophir ships. It is thought by some to be the sandalwood; by others, to be the deodar--a species of fragrant fir, much used in India for sacred and important works. Solomon used it for stairs in his temple and palace (<reference osisRef="2Chr.9.11">2Ch 9:11</reference>), but chiefly for musical instruments. <div eID="gen4468" type="x-p"/>
entries.708e4b8d46cc3f98c7dd3be710f737083868cddb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3198"/><div sID="gen4469" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3198"/><hi type="bold">13. King Solomon gave unto the queen of Sheba all her desire, whatsoever she asked, beside--</hi>that is, Solomon not only gave his illustrious guest all the insight and information she wanted; but, according to the Oriental fashion, he gave her ample remuneration for the presents she had brought.<div eID="gen4469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4470" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.14-1Kgs.10.29">1Ki 10:14-29</reference>. His Riches. <div eID="gen4470" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a5fb24ac5c97f9f16de9c203d2acc93a5e4b369: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3199"/><div sID="gen4471" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3199"/><hi type="bold">14-15. Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year--</hi>666 talents, equal to £3,996,000. The sources whence this was derived are not mentioned; nor was it the full amount of his revenue; for this was "Beside that he had of the merchantmen, and of the traffic of the spice merchants, and of all the kings of Arabia, and of the governors of the country." The great encouragement he gave to commerce was the means of enriching his royal treasury. By the fortifications which he erected in various parts of his kingdom, (particularly at such places as Thapsacus, one of the passages of Euphrates, and at Tadmor, in the Syrian desert), he gave complete security to the caravan trade from the depredations of the Arab marauders; and it was reasonable that, in return for this protection, he should exact a certain toll or duty for the importation of foreign goods. A considerable revenue, too, would arise from the use of the store cities and khans he built; and it is not improbable that those cities were emporia, where the caravan merchants unloaded their bales of spices and other commodities and sold them to the king's factors, who, according to the modern practice in the East, retailed them in the Western markets at a profit. "The revenue derived from the tributary kings and from the governors of the country" must have consisted in the tribute which all inferior magistrates periodically bring to their sovereigns in the East, in the shape of presents of the produce of their respective provinces. <div eID="gen4471" type="x-p"/>
entries.27c689c1cce657a75c0946ca19b08122b7dd5bae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3200"/><div sID="gen4472" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3200"/><hi type="bold">16-17. two hundred targets, six hundred shekels--</hi>These defensive arms were anciently made of wood and covered with leather; those were covered with fine gold. 600 shekels were used in the gilding of each target--300 for each shield. They were intended for the state armory of the palace (see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.26">1Ki 14:26</reference>). <div eID="gen4472" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e2f90dcec524e8bb8e9f7f2ee1e660580c6cd2b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3201"/><div sID="gen4473" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3201"/><hi type="bold">18-26. a great throne of ivory--</hi>It seems to have been made not of solid ivory, but veneered. It was in the form of an armchair, with a carved back. The ascent to it was by six steps, on each of which stood lions, in place of a railing--while a lion, probably of gilt metal, stood at each side, which, we may suppose from the analogy of other Oriental thrones, supported a canopy. A golden footstool is mentioned (<reference osisRef="2Chr.9.18">2Ch 9:18</reference>) as attached to this throne, whose magnificence is described as unrivalled. <div eID="gen4473" type="x-p"/>

entries.835c2705d112ec3dd248a70183ea94284f3a0c50: <div eID="gen11785" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen11786" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11787" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11787" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11786" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11788" type="x-p"/> The queen of Sheba visits Solomon, and brings rich presents; and tries him by hard questions, which he readily solves, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.1-1Kgs.10.3">1Kgs 10:1-3</reference>. She expresses great surprise at his wisdom, his buildings, his court, etc.; and praises God for placing him on the Jewish throne, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.4-1Kgs.10.9">1Kgs 10:4-9</reference>. She gives him rich presents, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.10">1Kgs 10:10</reference>. What the navy of Hiram brought from Ophir, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.11">1Kgs 10:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.12">1Kgs 10:12</reference>. The queen of Sheba returns, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.13">1Kgs 10:13</reference>. Solomon's annual revenue, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.14">1Kgs 10:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.15">1Kgs 10:15</reference>. He makes two hundred targets and three hundred shields of gold, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.16">1Kgs 10:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.17">1Kgs 10:17</reference>. His magnificent ivory throne, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.18-1Kgs.10.20">1Kgs 10:18-20</reference>. His drinking vessels all of gold, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.21">1Kgs 10:21</reference>. What the navy of Tharshish brought every three years to Solomon, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.22">1Kgs 10:22</reference>. His great riches, numerous chariots, and horsemen, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.23-1Kgs.10.27">1Kgs 10:23-27</reference>. He brings chariots and horses out of Egypt, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.28">1Kgs 10:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.29">1Kgs 10:29</reference>. <div eID="gen11788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11789" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen11789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11790" type="x-p"/> When the queen of Sheba heard - As our Lord calls her queen of the south, (<reference osisRef="Mat.12.42">Mat 12:42</reference>), it is likely the name should be written Saba, Azab, or Azaba, all of which signify the south. She is called Balkis by the Arabians, but by the Abyssinians Maqueda. See the account at the end of this chapter, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.29">1Kgs 10:29</reference> (note). <div eID="gen11790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11791" type="x-p"/> With hard questions - בחידות bechidoth; Septuagint, εν αινιγμασι, riddles. With parables and riddles, says the Arabic.
entries.df11f960c20257d3f6c7056c7d11cd0a81e88ba1: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen11791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11792" type="x-p"/> She came to Jerusalem with - spices, etc. - Those who contend that she was queen of the Sabaeans, a people of Arabia Felix, towards the southern extremity of the Red Sea, find several proofs of their opinion: <div eID="gen11792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11793" type="x-p"/> 1. That the Sabaeans abounded in riches and spices. <div eID="gen11793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11794" type="x-p"/> India mittit ebur, molles sua thura Sabaei "India furnishes ivory, and the effeminate Sabaeans their frankincense." <div eID="gen11794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11795" type="x-p"/> Virg. Geor. i., ver. 57. <div eID="gen11795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11796" type="x-p"/> And again: - <div eID="gen11796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11797" type="x-p"/> Divisae arboribus patriae: sola India nigrum <div eID="gen11797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11798" type="x-p"/> Fert ebenum; solis est thurea virga Sabaeis. <div eID="gen11798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11799" type="x-p"/> Geor. ii., ver. 116. <div eID="gen11799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11800" type="x-p"/> All sorts of trees their several countries know: <div eID="gen11800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11801" type="x-p"/> Black ebon only will in India grow; <div eID="gen11801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11802" type="x-p"/> And odorous frankincense on the Sabaean bough. <div eID="gen11802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11803" type="x-p"/> Dryden. - Ubi templum illi centumque Sabaeo Thure calent arae. <div eID="gen11803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11804" type="x-p"/> Where to her fame a hundred altars rise, <div eID="gen11804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11805" type="x-p"/> And pour Sabaean odours to the skies. <div eID="gen11805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11806" type="x-p"/> Pliny (Hist. Nat. lib. xii., c. 17) observes, <div eID="gen11806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11807" type="x-p"/> Non alia ligni genera in usu sunt quam odorata; cibosque Sabaei coquunt thuris ligno; alii myrrhae. "The Sabaeans use odorous wood only, and even use the incense tree and myrrh to cook their victuals." <div eID="gen11807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11808" type="x-p"/> 2. All ancient authors speak, not only of their odoriferous woods, but of their rich gold and silver mines, and of their precious stones. See Pliny, Hist. Nat. lib. xxxvii., c. 6, etc. <div eID="gen11808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11809" type="x-p"/> 3. It is also well known that the Sabaeans had queens for their sovereigns, and not kings. So Claudian, in Eutrop. lib. i. - Medis levibusque Sabaeis Imperat hic sexus, reginarumque sub armis Barbariae pars magna jacet. <div eID="gen11809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11810" type="x-p"/> By this is meant, says Mr. Bruce, the country between the tropic and mountains of Abyssinia, the country of shepherds, from berber, a shepherd. And he contends that these Sabaeans were a distinct people from the Ethiopians and the Arabs, and that Saba was a distinct state.
entries.dfe6ad8ce25037208dc2a57760c1721ffebf1956: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen11810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11811" type="x-p"/> Solomon told her all her questions - Riddles, problems, fables, apologues, etc., formed the principal part of the wisdom of the East; indeed they use and delight in them to the present day. See the case of Samson and his friends, <reference osisRef="Jdg.14.12">Jdg 14:12</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Jdg.14.14">Jdg 14:14</reference> (note), and the notes there.
entries.71ec8e7a4a5263dbf4a8bb6b90cd84a8472a78fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen11811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11812" type="x-p"/> Had seen all Solomon's wisdom - By the answers which he gave to her subtle questions. <div eID="gen11812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11813" type="x-p"/> And the house that he had built - Most probably his own house.
entries.648de1eb7bfd4274130d39a7534a9869ec02da39: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen11813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11814" type="x-p"/> The meat of his table - The immense supply of all kinds of food daily necessary for the many thousands which were fed at and from his table. See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.22-1Kgs.4.23">1Kgs 4:22-23</reference> (note). <div eID="gen11814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11815" type="x-p"/> And the sitting of his servants - The various orders and distinctions of his officers. <div eID="gen11815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11816" type="x-p"/> The attendance of his ministers - See the account of these and their attendance, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.1">1Kgs 4:1</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen11816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11817" type="x-p"/> And their apparel - The peculiarity of their robes, and their splendor and costliness. <div eID="gen11817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11818" type="x-p"/> And his cup-bearers - The original משקיו mashkaiv may as well be applied to his beverage, or to his drinking utensils, as to his cup-bearers. <div eID="gen11818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11819" type="x-p"/> And his ascent by which he went up - It seems very strange that the steps to the temple should be such a separate matter of astonishment. The original is ועלתו אשר יעלה בית יהוה which all the versions have translated, And the holocausts which he offered in the house of the Lord. The Vulgate, Septuagint, Chaldee, Syriac, and Arabic, all express this sense: so does the German translation of Luther, from which, in this place, we have most pitifully departed: And seine Brandopfer, die er in dem Hause des Herrn opferte; "And his burnt-offering which he offered in the house of the Lord." <div eID="gen11819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11820" type="x-p"/> There was no more spirit in her - She was overpowered with astonishment; she fainted. I have seen precisely the same effect produced; a lady who was herself an artist, viewing some exquisitely finished oriental paintings, was so struck with astonishment that she twice nearly fainted, and was obliged to leave the room. What happened to the queen of Sheba is a natural and not an uncommon effect which will be produced in a delicate sensible mind at the sight of rare and extraordinary productions of art. <div eID="gen11820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11821" type="x-p"/> Of the profusion of Solomon's sacrifices we have already had proof, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.63">1Kgs 8:63</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.25">1Kgs 9:25</reference>.
entries.5267fe328b16e4985c26c0f447b4d4f00565575c: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen11821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11822" type="x-p"/> Happy are thy men - All these are very natural expressions from a person in her state of mind.
entries.dbc3e6da775a717f609b6cbb1e51ecc93f8b4bd2: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen11822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11823" type="x-p"/> A hundred and twenty talents of gold - The worth of these one hundred and twenty talents of gold, according to Mr. Reynolds, is equal to 843,905. 10s. 4 3/4d. of our British sterling. But the spices and precious stones might have been yet of more value. After this verse the 13th should be read, which is here most evidently misplaced; and then the account of the queen of Sheba will be concluded, and that of Solomon's revenue will stand without interruption.
entries.a7962ffc3b5ad6a5188d1b3d8491569fe0dc9b39: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen11823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11824" type="x-p"/> Great plenty of almug trees - In the parallel place, <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.10">2Chr 9:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.11">2Chr 9:11</reference>, these are called algum trees, the ם mem and the ג gimel being transposed; probably the latter is the more correct orthography. What the algum trees were we do not exactly know. The Vulgate calls it ligna thyina, the thya or lignum vitae wood; and Mr. Parkhurst thinks that the original אלגומים algumim, comes from אל al, not, and גם gem, to fill; because the lignum vitae is of so close a texture that it can imbibe no water, and cannot be affected by wet weather. The Septuagint translate it ξυλα πυκινα, pine timber; the Syriac kaise dakisotho, probably cypress wood, or what the translators render ligna brasilica; the Arabic translates coloured wood, and subjoins a paraphrase, for that wood was by nature painted with various colors. Perhaps the Arabic comes nearest the truth; wood shaded of different colors, such as the rose wood and such like, which are brought to us from various parts of the East Indies. The whole passage as it stands in the Arabic is this: "And the ships of Hiram brought gold from the land of Hind, (India), and they carried also much coloured wood, (but this wood is naturally painted of various colors), and very precious jewels. And Solomon put some of that same painted wood which was brought to him in the house of the Lord, and in his own house; and with it he adorned them." And for inlaying and veneering nothing can be finer than this wood.
entries.47bff08308e200f1fb48fab5247c1146626dbe91: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen11824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11825" type="x-p"/> All her desire whatsoever she asked - Some imagine she desired progeny from the wise king of Israel; and all the traditions concerning her state that she had a son by Solomon called Menilek, who was brought up at the Israelitish court, succeeded his mother in the kingdom of Saba, and introduced among his subjects the Jewish religion. See at the end of the chapter, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.29">1Kgs 10:29</reference> (note).
entries.a31cb9a65a8b324fbd4967f45b47c34e652a5dd6: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen11825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11826" type="x-p"/> The weight of gold - was six hundred threescore and six talents - This would amount in our money to 4,683, 675 12s. 8 1/2d. sterling. <div eID="gen11826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11827" type="x-p"/> This seems to be what he got annually of bullion; but independently of this, he had tribute of all the kings of Arabia, duties from merchantmen, and the traffic of spice merchants; see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.25">1Kgs 10:25</reference>.
entries.a47e2bb9b2819602b71b2418d14c29ecc430a91a: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen11827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11828" type="x-p"/> Solomon made two hundred targets of beaten gold - I have already conjectured that the צנה tsinnah might resemble the Highland targe or target, with a dagger projecting from the Umbo or center.
entries.eaa085b280f99f57460c185f6c71b9abe5f13d00: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen11828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11829" type="x-p"/> He made three hundred shields - The מגן magen was a large shield by which the whole body was protected. <div eID="gen11829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11830" type="x-p"/> Mr. Reynolds computes that the two hundred targets, on each of which were employed three hundred shekels of gold, were worth 28,131 16s. 9 1/2d. <div eID="gen11830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11831" type="x-p"/> And the three hundred shields, in forming each of which three pounds of gold were employed, were worth 210,976 7s. 7d.
entries.e30a745e474ff3567998b09255dcd0987e8963e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen11831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11832" type="x-p"/> The throne was round behind: and there were stays on either side - This description seems to indicate that the throne was in the form of one of our ancient round-topped, two-armed chairs. This throne or chair of state was raised on a platform, the ascent to which consisted of six steps. What we call stays is in the Hebrew ידת yadoth, hands, which serves to confirm the conjecture above.
entries.5706e8fdbdc4ef4131cc1c112097cd7b9a907d5a: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen11832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11833" type="x-p"/> A navy of Tharshish - For probable conjectures concerning this place, and the three years' voyage, see at the end of this, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.29">1Kgs 10:29</reference> (note) and the preceding chapter, 1 Kings 9 (note). <div eID="gen11833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11834" type="x-p"/> Apes - קפים kophim; probably a species of monkey rather than ape.
entries.2e597b1a5ec0087ad56946f0bcb2148cad85b84d: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen11834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11835" type="x-p"/> Solomon exceeded all the kings of the earth for riches - Mr. Reynolds, stating the yearly tribute of Solomon, 666 talents of gold, at about four times as much as his father left him, hence reckons that he had 4,909, 371 8s. 8d. each year, 94,410 19s. 9 1/4d. per week, 13,487 5s. 8d. per day, taking each day, week, and year, one with another.
entries.cf596d28086cfe47be4aaee121d520d332912056: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen11835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11836" type="x-p"/> They brought every man his present - This means tribute; and it shows us of what sort that tribute was, viz., vessels of gold and silver, probably ingots; garments of very rich stuffs; armor, for little of this kind was ever made in Judea; spices, which doubtless sold well in that country; horses, which were very rare; and mules, the most necessary animal for all the purposes of life.
entries.8b2d4a29c51125dfcd3dbd0c8866bcd92cd09742: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen11836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11837" type="x-p"/> He had a thousand and four hundred chariots - See the note on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.26">1Kgs 4:26</reference>.
entries.f44ecc8bc3a435d6a07fe72ab32ac60f120a6664: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen11837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11838" type="x-p"/> Made silver - as stones - He destroyed its value by making it so exceedingly plenty. <div eID="gen11838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11839" type="x-p"/> As the sycamore trees - He planted many cedars, and doubtless had much cedar wood imported; so that it became as common as the sycamore trees, which appear to have grown there in great abundance. This is considered to be a tree that partakes of the nature of the fig tree, and of the mulberry. Of the former it has the fruit, and of the latter the leaves; that is, the fruit had a considerable resemblance to the fig, and the leaf to that of the mulberry tree: hence its name sycamore, from the Greek συκον, a fig, and μορεα, a mulberry tree.
entries.bf25c3ae4f33b3bcc9934dae8bf12d2dd41e2ce1: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen11839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11840" type="x-p"/> Horses brought out of Egypt - It is thought that the first people who used horses in war were the Egyptians; and it is well known that the nations who knew the use of this creature in battle had greatly the advantage of those who did not. God had absolutely prohibited horses to be imported or used; but in many things Solomon paid little attention to the Divine command. <div eID="gen11840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11841" type="x-p"/> And linen yarn - The original word, מקוה mikveh, is hard to be understood, if it be not indeed a corruption. <div eID="gen11841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11842" type="x-p"/> The versions are all puzzled with it: the Vulgate and Septuagint make it a proper name: "And Solomon had horses brought out of Egypt, and from Coa, or Tekoa." Some think it signifies a tribute, thus Bochart: "They brought horses to Solomon out of Egypt; and as to the tribute, the farmers of this prince received it at a price." They farmed the tribute, gave so much annually for it, taking the different kinds to themselves, and giving a round sum for the whole. <div eID="gen11842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11843" type="x-p"/> Some suppose that Mikveh signifies the string or cord by which one horse's head is tied to the tail of another; and that the meaning is, Solomon brought droves of horses, thus tied, out of Egypt. <div eID="gen11843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11844" type="x-p"/> Rabbi Solomon Jarchi, in his comment on the parallel place, <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.14">2Chr 1:14</reference>, says that מקוה mikveh signifies a collection or drove of horses, or what the Germans call stutte, a stud. He observes on that place, "That he has heard that there was a company of merchants in Egypt, who bought horses from the Egyptians at a certain price, on condition that no person should be permitted to bring a horse out of Egypt but through them." Houbigant supposes the place to be corrupt, and that for מקוה mikveh we should read מרכבה mercabah, chariots: "And Solomon had horses brought out of Egypt, and chariots; and the king's merchants received the chariots at a price: and a chariot came up and went out of Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver," etc. This makes a very good and consistent sense; but none of the versions acknowledged it, nor is there any various reading here in any of the MSS. yet collated. <div eID="gen11844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11845" type="x-p"/> If we understand it of thread, it may refer to the byssus or fine flax for which Egypt was famous; but I do not see on what authority we translate it linen thread. Bochart's opinion appears to me the most probable, as the text now stands; but the charge contended for by Houbigant makes the text far more simple and intelligible.
entries.2fd8c9e11aa1e186e340d546000435607b364861: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen11845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11846" type="x-p"/> A chariot came up - for six hundred shekels - This was the ordinary price of a chariot, as a hundred and fifty shekels were for a horse. <div eID="gen11846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11847" type="x-p"/> Kings of the Hittites - These must have been the remains of the original inhabitants of Canaan, who had gone to some other country, probably Syria, and formed themselves into a principality there. It seems that neither horses nor chariots came out of Egypt but by means of Solomon's servants.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.10"/> <div eID="gen11847" type="x-p"/>

entries.3e98766af9b66c55d78135ec31ef6c1e72d06264: <div eID="gen4889" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">CHAP. X. THE QUEEN OF SABA. SOLOMON’S WEALTH AND SPLENDOUR.</title> <div sID="gen4890" type="x-p"/> Visit of the Queen of Saba (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.1-2Chr.9.12">2Ch 9:1-12</reference>). - When the fame of Solomon’s great wisdom came to the ears of the queen of Saba, probably through the Ophir voyages, she undertook a journey to Jerusalem, to convince herself of the truth of the report which had reached her, by putting it to the test by means of enigmas. שׁבא, Σαβά, is not Ethiopia or Meroë, as Josephus (<hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. viii. 6, 5), who confounds שׁבא with סבא, and the Abyssinian Christians suppose (vid., Ludolfi <hi type="italic">hist. Aeth</hi>. ii. 3), but the kingdom of the <hi type="italic">Sabaeans</hi>, who were celebrated for their trade in incense, gold, and precious stones, and who dwelt in Arabia Felix, with the capital <hi type="italic">Saba</hi>, or the Μαριάβα of the Greeks. This queen, who is called <hi type="italic">Balkis</hi> in the Arabian legend (cf. Koran, <hi type="italic">Sur</hi>. 27, and Pococke, <hi type="italic">Specim. hist. Arab</hi>. p. 60), heard the fame of Solomon יהוה לשׁם; i.e., not “at the naming of the name of Jehovah” (Böttcher), nor “in respect of the glory of the Lord, with regard to that which Solomon had instituted for the glory of the Lord” (Thenius); nor even “serving to the glorification of God” (de Wette and Maurer); but literally, “belonging to the name of the Lord:” in other words, the fame which Solomon had acquired through the name of the Lord, or through the fact that the Lord had so glorified Himself in him (Ewald and Dietrich in Ges. <hi type="italic">Lex. s.v</hi>. ל). “She came to try him with riddles,” i.e., to put his wisdom to the test by carrying on a conversation with him in riddles. The love of the Arabs for riddles, and their superiority in this <hi type="italic">jeu d’esprit</hi>, is sufficiently well known from the immense extent to which the Arabic literature abounds in <hi type="italic">Mashals</hi>. We have only to think of the large collections of proverbs made by Ali ben Abi Taleb and Meidani, or the <hi type="italic">Makamen</hi> of Hariri, which have been made accessible to all by F. Rückert’s masterly translation into German, and which are distinguished by an amazing fulness of word-play and riddles. חידה, a riddle, is a pointed saying which merely hints at the deeper truth and leaves it to be guessed.
entries.87245f4aa0489f9464bbd9edd02f0cc5ff9a293c: 1Ki 10:2-3 <div eID="gen4890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4891" type="x-p"/> As the queen of a wealthy country, she came with a very large retinue. חיל does not mean a military force or an armed escort (Thenius), but riches, property; namely, her numerous retinue of men (עבדים, 1Ki 10:13), and camels laden with valuable treasures. The words יקרה...גּמלּים are an explanatory circumstantial clause, both here and also in the Chronicles, where the cop. <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> stands before גּמלּים (cf. Ewald, §341, <hi type="italic">a</hi>., <hi type="italic">b</hi>.). “And spake to Solomon all that she had upon her heart,” i.e., in this connection, whatever riddles she had it in her mind to lay before him; “and Solomon told her all her sayings,” i.e., was able to solve all her riddles. There is no ground for thinking of sayings of a religious nature, as the earlier commentators supposed, but simply of sayings the meaning of which was concealed, and the understanding of which indicated very deep wisdom.
entries.ddc32a93ce94b7c8046bd443db00f5fdba4b4668: 1Ki 10:4-5 <div eID="gen4891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4892" type="x-p"/> She saw הבּית, i.e., Solomon’s palace, not the temple, and “the food of his table,” i.e., both the great variety of food that was placed upon the king’s table (1Ki 5:2-3), and also the costly furniture of the table (1Ki 10:21), and “the seat of his retainers and the standing of his servants,” i.e., the places in the palace assigned to the ministers and servants of the king, which were contrived with wisdom and arranged in a splendid manner. עבדים are the chief officers of the king, viz., ministers, counsellors, and <hi type="italic">aides de camp</hi>; משׁרתים, the court servants; מושׁב, the rooms of the courtiers in attendance; מעמד, the standing-place, i.e., the rooms of the inferior servants, “and their clothing,” which they received from the king; and משׁקיו, not his cup-bearers (lxx, Vulg.), but as in <reference osisRef="Gen.40.21">Gen 40:21</reference>, the drink, i.e., probably the whole of the drinking arrangements; ועלתו, and his ascent, by which he was accustomed to go into the house of Jehovah. עלה does not mean burnt-offering here, as the older translators have rendered it, but ascent, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.26">Eze 40:26</reference>, and as the Chronicles have correctly explained it by עליּתו. For burnt-offering is not to be thought of in this connection, because the queen had nothing to see or to be astonished at in the presentation of such an offering. עלתו is most likely “the king’s outer entrance” into the temple, mentioned in 2Ki 16:18; and the passage before us would lead us to suppose that this was a work of art, or an artistic arrangement. וגו היה ולא, “and there was no more spirit in her:” she was beside herself with amazement, as in <reference osisRef="Josh.5.1">Jos 5:1</reference>; Jos 2:11.
entries.0c92ca4b4b8e5435c65b67474f3ca4b2d49185d1: 1Ki 10:6-9 <div eID="gen4892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4893" type="x-p"/> She then said with astonishment to Solomon, that of what her eyes now saw she had not heard the half, through the report which had reached her of his affairs and of his wisdom, and which had hitherto appeared incredible to her; and not only congratulated his servants, who stood continually near him and could hear his wisdom, but also praised Jehovah his God, that out of His eternal love to His people Israel He had given them a king to do justice and righteousness. The earlier theologians inferred from this praising of Jehovah, which involved faith in the true God, when taken in connection with <reference osisRef="Matt.12.42">Mat 12:42</reference>, that this queen had been converted to the true God, and conversed with Solomon on religious matters. But, as we have already observed at 1Ki 5:7, an acknowledgment of Jehovah as the God of Israel was reconcilable with polytheism. And the fact that nothing is said about her offering sacrifice in the temple, shows that the conversion of the queen is not to be thought of here.
entries.04f309237827760d0b11ed0cb502981189387acc: 1Ki 10:10 <div eID="gen4893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4894" type="x-p"/> She thereupon presented to Solomon a hundred and twenty talents of gold (more than three million thalers nearly half a million sterling - Tr.]), and a very large quantity of spices and precious stones. The בּשׂמים probably included the genuine balsam of Arabia, even if בּשׂם was not the specific name of the genuine balsam. “There never more came so much of such spices of Jerusalem.” Instead of לרב עוד...בּא לא we find in the Chronicles, 1Ki 10:9, simply היה לא, “there was nothing like this balsam,” which conveys the same meaning though expressed more indefinitely, since ההוּא ecni כּבּשׂם points back to the preceding words, “balsam (spices) in great quantity.”<note placement="foot">It was this which gave rise to the legend in Josephus (<hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. viii. 6, 6), that it was through this queen that the root of the true balsam (<hi type="italic">Opobalsamum</hi>), which was afterwards cultivated in gardens at Jericho and Engedi, was first of all brought to Palestine (cf. Movers, <hi type="italic">Phönizier</hi>, ii. 3, p. 226ff.</note>.
entries.3dbc8db482d1c40cee1fcd6b2b8c29eb394b7d89: 1Ki 10:11-12 <div eID="gen4894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4895" type="x-p"/> The allusion to these costly presents leads the historian to introduce the remark here, that the Ophir fleet also brought, in addition to gold, a large quantity of <hi type="italic">Algummim</hi> wood (see at 1Ki 9:28) and precious stones. Of this wood Solomon had מסעד or מסלּות made for the temple and palace. מסעד, from סעד, signifies a support, and מסלּה may be a later form for סלּם, a flight of steps or a staircase, so that we should have to think of steps with bannisters. This explanation is at any rate a safer one than that of “divans” (Thenius), which would have been quite out of place in the temple, or “narrow pannelled stripes on the floor” (Bertheau), which cannot in the smallest degree be deduced from מסעד, or “support = moveables, viz., tables, benches, footstools, boxes, and drawers” (Böttcher), which neither harmonizes with the temple, where there was no such furniture, nor with the מסלּות of the Chronicles. “And guitars and harps for the singers,” probably for the temple singers. כּנּור and נבל are string instruments; the former resembling our guitar rather than the harp, the strings being carried over the sounding-board upon a bridge, the latter being of a pitcher shape without any sounding bridge, as in the case of the harps.
entries.93142b04fec12f3dea2ba40d4095ecf0f980f8de: 1Ki 10:13 <div eID="gen4895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4896" type="x-p"/> Solomon gave the queen of Saba all that she wished and asked for, beside what he gave her “according to the hand,” i.e., the might, of the king; that is to say, in addition to the presents answering to his might and his wealth, which he was obliged to give as a king, according to the Oriental custom. In the Chronicles (1Ki 10:12) we find “beside that which she had brought (הביאה) to the king,” which is an abbreviated expression for “beside that which he gave her in return for what she had brought to him,” or beside the return presents corresponding to her gifts to him, as it has been already correctly paraphrased by the Targum.
entries.baae3bbca92c8df155e96d157abdaa24b9d3e5f7: 1Ki 10:14-15 <div eID="gen4896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4897" type="x-p"/> Solomon’s Wealth and the Use He Made of It (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.13-2Chr.9.21">2Ch 9:13-21</reference>). - 1Ki 10:14. The gold which Solomon received in one year amounted to 666 talents, - more than seventeen million thalers (two million and a half sterling - Tr.). 666 is evidently a round number founded upon an approximative valuation. אחת בּשׁנה is rendered in the Vulg. <hi type="italic">per annos singulos</hi>; but this is hardly correct, as the Ophir fleet, the produce of which is at any rate included, did not arrive every year, but once in three years. Thenius is wrong in supposing that this revenue merely applies to the direct taxes levied upon the Israelites. It includes all the branches of Solomon’s revenue, whether derived from his commerce by sea and land (cf. 1Ki 10:28, 1Ki 10:29) or from the royal domains (<reference osisRef="1Chr.27.26-1Chr.27.31">1Ch 27:26-31</reference>), or received in the form of presents from foreign princes, who either visited him like the queen of Saba or sent ambassadors to him (1Ki 10:23, 1Ki 10:24), excepting the duties and tribute from conquered kings, which are specially mentioned in 1Ki 10:15.   הת מאנשׁי לבד, beside what came in (לשׁלמה בּא) from the travelling traders and the commerce of the merchants, and from all the kings, etc. התּרים אנשׁי (a combination resembling our merchantmen; cf. Ewald, §287, e., p. 721) are probably the tradesmen or smaller dealers who travelled about in the country, and רכלים the wholesale dealers. This explanation of תּרים cannot be rendered doubtful by the objection that תּוּר only occurs elsewhere in connection with the wandering about of spies; for רכל signified originally to go about, spy out, or retail scandal, and after that to trade, and go about as a tradesman. הערב מלכי are not kings of the auxiliary and allied nations (Chald., Ges.), but kings of the mixed population, and according to <reference osisRef="Jer.25.24">Jer 25:24</reference>, more especially of the population of Arabia Deserta (בּמּדבּר השּׁכנים), which bordered upon Palestine; for ערב rof is a mixed crowd of all kinds of men, who either attach themselves to a nation (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.38">Exo 12:38</reference>), or live in the midst of it as foreigners (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.3">Neh 13:3</reference>), hence a number of mercenaries (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.37">Jer 50:37</reference>). In <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.14">2Ch 9:14</reference>, הערב is therefore correctly explained by the term ערב, which does not mean the whole of Arabia, but “only a tract of country not very extensive on the east and south of Palestine” (Gesenius), as these tribes were tributary of Solomon. הארץ פּחות, the governors of the land, are probably the officers named in 1Ki 4:7-19. As they collected the duties in the form of natural productions and delivered them in that form, so also did the tradesmen and merchants pay their duties, and the subjugated pastoral tribes of Arabia their tribute, <hi type="italic">in natura</hi>. This explains in a very simple manner why these revenues are separated from the revenue of Solomon which came in the form of money. פּחה is a foreign word, which first found its way into the Hebrew language after the times of the Assyrians, and sprang from the Sanscrit <hi type="italic">paksha</hi>, a companion or friend, which took the form of <hi type="italic">pakkha</hi> in Prakrit, and probably of <hi type="italic">pakha</hi> in the early Persian (vid., Benfey and Stern, <hi type="italic">die Monatsnamen</hi>, p. 195).
entries.716762cd5d47d65cd3d89ca184201e2258a2e61d: 1Ki 10:16-17 <div eID="gen4897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4898" type="x-p"/> Solomon had 500 ornamental shields made, 200 larger ones (צנּים, <hi type="italic">scuta</hi>, targets), and 300 smaller (מגנּים, <hi type="italic">clypei</hi>). These shields, like all the shields of the ancients, were made of wood or basket-work, and covered with gold plate instead of leather (see my <hi type="italic">bibl. Archäol</hi>. ii. pp. 296ff.). שׁחוּט זהב does not mean <hi type="italic">aurum jugulatum</hi>, i.e., gold mixed with metal of a different kind, but, as Kimchi has shown, <hi type="italic">aurum diductum</hi>, beaten gold, from שׁחט, to stretch; since Solomon would certainly use pure gold for these ornamental shields. “Six hundred shekels of gold he spread upon one target,” that is to say, he used for gilding one target. Six hundred shekels would weigh about 17 1/2 lbs., so that the value of the gold upon a target would be more than 5000 thalers (£750), supposing that the Mosaic shekel is meant. But this is rendered doubtful by the fact that the gold upon the small shields is estimated at three minae. If, for example, the three minae are equal to three hundred shekels, according to <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.16">2Ch 9:16</reference>, as is generally assumed, a hundred shekels are reckoned as one mina; and as the mina only contained fifty Mosaic shekels, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.12">Eze 45:12</reference>, the reference must be to shekels after the king’s weight (<reference osisRef="2Sam.14.26">2Sa 14:26</reference>), which were only half the sacred shekels (see my <hi type="italic">bibl. Archäol</hi>. ii. p. 135). Consequently the gold plate upon one target was not quite 9 lbs., and that upon a shield not quite 4 1/2 lbs. These shields were intended for the body-guard to carry on state occasions (1Ki 14:27-28; <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.10">2Ch 12:10</reference>), and were kept in the house of the forest of Lebanon (1Ki 7:2).
entries.262aad62bb0ba193685203dff71401d86726f947: 1Ki 10:18-20 <div eID="gen4898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4899" type="x-p"/> Solomon had a great throne of ivory made, and had it overlaid with fine gold. כּסּא־שׁן is not a throne made of ivory, but one merely ornamented with ivory; and we are to imagine the gilding as effected by laying the gold simply upon the wood, and inserting the ivory within the gold plate. מוּפז, a <hi type="italic">hophal</hi> participle of פּזז: <hi type="italic">aurum depuratum</hi>, hence = טהור in 2Ch 9:17. The throne had six steps, and a “rounded head on the hinder part thereof,” i.e., a back which was arched above or rounded off,<note placement="foot">Instead of מאחריו לכּסּה עגול וראשׁ we have in the Chronicles מאחזים לכּסּא בּזּהב וכבשׁ, “and a footstool in gold fastened to the throne” (the plural מאחזים refers to the footstool and the steps). Now, however easily מאחזים may have been written by mistake for מאחריו, זהב כבשׁ cannot have grown out of עגול ראשׁ by any such mistake. The <hi type="italic">quid-pro-quo</hi> of the lxx for עגול rof xxl  ראשׁ, προτομαὶ μόσχων, in which עגול is certainly confounded with עגל, does not warrant the conjecture of Thenius, that the Chronicler found עגל in his original and substituted כּבשׂ (lamb), whereupon כּבשׂ (lamb) was changed by another hand into כּבשׁ footstep, and ראשׁ was dropped altogether.</note> and ירת, arms, i.e., arms on both sides of the seat (השּׁבת מקום), and two lions standing by the side of the arms. Beside this there were twelve lions upon the six steps, namely two upon each step, one on this side and one on that. Instead of אריים (1Ki 10:20) we find ארירת in 1Ki 10:19, just as we do in both verses of the Chronicles, not because the reference is to artificial, inanimate figures and not to natural lions, as Thenius supposes, but because the plural ending  ים- is an unusual one with this word; and even where natural lions are spoken of, we always find ארירת in other passages (cf. Jdg 14:5; <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.23">2Sa 1:23</reference>; 2Ki 17:25; Sol 4:8, etc.). The lions were symbols of the ruler’s authority; and the twelve lions upon the steps may possibly have pointed to the rule over the twelve tribes of Israel, which was concentrated in the throne; not “watchers of the throne,” as Thenius thinks. This throne was so splendid a work, that the historian observes that nothing of the kind had ever been made for any other kingdom. Upon the early Assyrian monuments we do indeed find high seats depicted, which are very artistically worked, and provided with backs and arms, and some with the arms supported by figures of animals (see Layard’s <hi type="italic">Nineveh and its Remains</hi>, vol. ii. p. 301), but none resembling Solomon’s throne. It is not till a later age that the more splendid thrones appear (vid., Rosenmüller, <hi type="italic">A. u. N. Morgenland</hi>, iii. pp. 176ff.).
entries.2dd914f2794c0c78d2ffe63ef95722aed3524165: 1Ki 10:21-22 <div eID="gen4899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4900" type="x-p"/> The drinking vessels of Solomon also were all of gold, and all the vessels of the house of the forest of Lebanon of costly gold (סגוּר: see at 1Ki 6:20). Silver was counted as nothing, because the Tarshish fleet arrived once in three years, bringing gold, silver, etc. (see at 1Ki 9:28). <div eID="gen4900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4901" type="x-p"/> In 1Ki 10:23-29 everything that had to be stated concerning the wealth, wisdom, and revenue of Solomon is summed up as conclusion (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.22-2Chr.9.28">2Ch 9:22-28</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.14-2Chr.1.17">2Ch 1:14-17</reference>).
entries.b3a54e87ce7b9a45eb6034cfcb98d62167d4100b: 1Ki 10:23-25 1Ki 10:23, 1Ki 10:24 point back to 1Ki 5:9-14. ויּגדּל: Solomon became greater, not was greater, on account of the <hi type="italic">Vâv consec</hi>. כּל־הארץ, all the world, corresponds to כּל־העמּים in 1Ki 5:14. The foreigners out of all lands, who came on account of his wisdom, brought Solomon presents: gold and silver vessels, clothes (שׂלמות, court dresses, which are still customary presents in the East), נשׁק, armour, spices, horses and mules.
entries.8764721e71a645ff3823c771d72600eb375c1cc5: 1Ki 10:26-27 1Ki 10:26 is simply a repetition of 1Ki 5:6 (compare also 1Ki 9:19); and 1Ki 10:27 is merely a further extension of 1Ki 10:21. The words of 1Ki 10:27, “Solomon made silver like stones in Jerusalem, and cedars like the sycamores in the lowland for abundance,” are a hyperbolical description of his collection of enormous quantities of precious metals and costly wood. שׁקמים, <hi type="italic">sycomori</hi>, mulberry fig-trees, are very rare in Palestine in its present desolate state (see Rob. <hi type="italic">Pal</hi>. iii. 27), and are only met in any abundance in Egypt; but in ancient times they abounded in the lowlands of Palestine to such an extent, that they were used as common building wood (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.9.9">Isa 9:9</reference>, on which Theodoret observes, τούτων (συκαμίνων) ἡ Παλαιστίνη πεπλήρωται). According to <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.28">1Ch 27:28</reference>, the sycamore forests in the lowland of Judah were royal domains.
entries.ddb0b6ab03cff356fe8b5dd3b34349b374a42e82: 1Ki 10:28-29 (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.16-2Chr.1.17">2Ch 1:16-17</reference>). “And (as for) the going out of horses from Egypt for Solomon, a company of king’s merchants fetched (horses) for a definite price.” This is the only possible explanation of the verse according to the Masoretic punctuation; but to obtain it, the first מקוה must be connected with סחרי in opposition to the accents, and the second must be pointed מקוה. This is the rendering adopted by Gesenius in his <hi type="italic">Thesaurus</hi> and <hi type="italic">Lexicon</hi> (ed. Dietr. <hi type="italic">s. v</hi>. מקוה). The meaning company or troop may certainly be justified from <reference osisRef="Gen.1.10">Gen 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.7.19">Exo 7:19</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Lev.11.36">Lev 11:36</reference>, where the word signifies an accumulation of water. Still there is something very strange not only in the application of the word both to a company of traders and also to a troop of horses, but also in the omission of סוּסים (horses) after the second מקוה. Hence the rendering of the lxx and Vulgate deserves attention, and may possibly be the one to be preferred (as Michaelis, Bertheau <hi type="italic">on Chron</hi>., and Movers assume). The translators of these versions have taken מקוה as the name of a place, ἐξ Ἐκουέ, or rather ἐκ Κουέ, <hi type="italic">de Coa</hi>.<note placement="foot">That Κουέ or Κωέ is the earliest reading of the lxx, and not the ἐκ Θεκουέ of the Cod. Vat. and Alex., is very evident from the statement which we find in the <hi type="italic">Onomast</hi>. of Eusebius (<hi type="italic">ed. Larsow et Parth</hi>. p. 260), Κώδ, πλησίον Αἰγύπτου; for which Jerome has <hi type="italic">Coa, quae est juxta Aegyptum</hi>, after the Vulgate.</note> <div eID="gen4901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4902" type="x-p"/> According to this, the rendering would be: “And as for the going out of horses from Egypt and Koa (or Kawe) for Solomon, the king’s traders fetched them from Joa (Kawe) for a fixed price.” It is true that the situation of <hi type="italic">Koa</hi> cannot be more precisely defined; but there seems to be very little doubt that it was a place for the collection of customs upon the frontier of Egypt.
